claims.text: The target materials are nanoparticles containing five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and initially forming a homogeneous single-phase solid solution.
Substituting a constituent metal with an element having a closer atomic radius can reduce atomic size mismatch while retaining equiatomic ratios.
The modified and control nanoparticles will be exposed under otherwise identical conditions over 473–1923 K for extended periods.
Atomic diffusion kinetics are governed by diffusion activation energy.
Atomic size mismatch influences diffusion activation energy in these multimetallic nanoparticles.
Reducing atomic size mismatch increases the diffusion activation energy.
A higher diffusion barrier restrains atomic mobility.
Restraining atomic mobility delays phase segregation and chemical ordering.
Phase segregation and chemical ordering can arise through atomistic rearrangement in multicomponent alloys.
Suppressing segregation and chemical ordering helps preserve the initial single-phase solid solution.
Nanoparticles with reduced atomic size mismatch will retain structural and chemical stability longer than the original control.
Nanoparticles with higher atomic size mismatch will exhibit an earlier onset of phase segregation or chemical ordering.
The reduced-mismatch nanoparticles will maintain a single-phase solid solution across 473–1923 K.
The original equiatomic control may undergo diffusion-driven phase changes at high temperature.
A nearly equiatomic multicomponent solid solution can remain single-phase at elevated temperature.
Mixing enthalpy may also affect the rate or threshold temperature of phase segregation.
The prediction applies only when oxidation, severe mechanical stress, and other nonthermal environmental effects do not significantly alter diffusion behavior.
X-ray diffraction, TEM, EDS mapping, and optional diffusion measurements will be used to compare phase evolution, nanostructure, elemental segregation, and diffusion kinetics.
Failure of the reduced-mismatch material to show delayed or reduced segregation and ordering relative to the control would falsify the hypothesis.
